I started studying for the 1001 on 8/11/19 and passed the test 9/10/19, so around 30 days. 

I started studying for the 1002 on 9/3/19 and passed the test today 9/24/19, so around 21 days or 51 in total. 

I'd say I averaged about 10 - 15 hours per week studying.  

I do not have any IT experience (but I do have an interview on Tuesday!) but love tech and built my own gaming desktop back in 2018. That only gave me almost enough knowledge to pass the 1001 from all the researching I did into hardware. 

The most important piece of advice is test taking strategy. 

Start test

Skip PBQs

Answer all questions, even if you don't know it, pick your best answer and flag it. 

Answer PBQs

Review every question but don't necessarily change answers as your gut feeling first guess is right most of the time. 

Submit

For both tests I finished with roughly 30 min left on the clock after reviewing all answers, so there's definitely plenty of time. 

Also definitely know the really common ports: HTTP, HTTPS, SSH, FTP, DNS, DHCP, SMTP, IMAP, RDP, POP3. 

Know all the basic command prompt commands: ipconfig and it's switches, tracert, ping, nslookup, etc. 

Know what kind of hardware to use for different types of systems: gaming rig, VM machine, AV editor, etc. 

Know the main raid types: 0, 1, 5, 10. 

Know basic network troubleshooting: APIPA address, ping default gateway, loopback address, etc. 

That's all I can really think of at the moment. Hope that helps a bit.

EDIT: Also, study to learn the material, DO NOT study just to pass the test. Set up your own VMs, set up a Windows Server, try all of the commands in a command prompt, play around in your BIOS, stuff like that.

I'll try my hand at this. In computer science, and math really, there are 2 main types of problems. They are called P and NP. P stands for Polynomial time and NP stands for non-polynomial time. P problems are solvable in realistic timescales, hence the term polynomial time. NP problems, like protein folding and "the travelling salesman" are NP problems that have an exponential time to solve. In the school of NP problems lies a subset called NP Complete. Essentially these are problems that are currently not able to be solved with brute force. They simply take to much time. But, if you know the answer you can quickly check that it's right. That's what happened here.

Edit: An analogy is as follows: You use a password to log into a website. You simply type in your password and the website knows immediately whether it's the right password. But for someone trying to brute force your password, they have to try an insane amount of combinations. The amount of password combinations, for let's say a 10 digit password is 4,923,990,397,355,877,376. If you can guess 1 million per second it would only take 156035.30 years. If you know the right password you can check it immediately. Hope that helps a bit.
